findings.text: The old code escaped every ESC char to ``. The new code only strips complete `ESC[...m` color sequences. Any other ESC byte survives, such as cursor codes like `ESC[2K` or `ESC[1A`, or a bare ESC. Raw 0x1B is invalid in XML 1.0, so the JUnit file is malformed and parsers will reject it. This is a regression, for example for test output containing `\033[K`.

`${output//${BASH_REMATCH[0]}/}` uses the matched text as a glob pattern. It is unquoted, so `[0-9;]` in the match acts as a bracket expression instead of a literal. For input `ESC[1m`, the pattern `ESC[1m` matches ESC followed by '1' or 'm', not the full sequence. That leaves `[`... in the output, and the loop may not remove the sequence correctly. It can also loop forever if the pattern never matches the literal text.

1.reason: The matched text can only contain ESC, '[', digits, ';' and 'm', so it never has a closing ']'; bash glob treats an unclosed '[' as a literal, so the unquoted pattern removes the exact sequence and the loop ends.
